name: shadcn/ui
definition: shadcn/ui provides open-source UI components and tooling for distributing component code that teams can add to their projects and customize. The editable implementations become part of the consuming codebase.
contentMarkdown:
# shadcn/ui

shadcn/ui provides open-source UI components and tooling for distributing component code that teams can add to their projects and customize. The editable implementations become part of the consuming codebase.

## How does the component approach work?

The project supplies component source that becomes part of the consuming codebase. Teams can inspect and modify that implementation for their own requirements.

This changes the maintenance responsibility. A local customization needs review when upstream behavior, dependencies, or project requirements change. Adding a component is not the same as delegating all future maintenance to a package publisher.

The component may still depend on other libraries. Inspect the actual dependencies and implementation selected for the project.

## What is a shadcn registry?

A registry describes distributable items and the files and dependencies they need. It can provide components, larger blocks, and other project material.

An organization can use a registry to distribute its own approved implementations. The registry is a distribution mechanism; it does not establish that every item meets the organization's design, security, or accessibility requirements.

## How does it work with AI tools?

The shadcn MCP server lets a connected assistant browse, search, and install items from configured registries. This can help an agent find an existing implementation instead of inventing a new component.

Specify which registry and project conventions to use. Review the actual files and dependency changes before accepting a generated implementation. Natural-language installation does not remove that responsibility.

## Example: building a settings dialog

Suppose a team adds a dialog and form fields, then adapts their styling to the product's tokens. It checks labels, focus behavior, validation, saving, and failure recovery in the settings task.

If the team later changes the dialog's behavior locally, it records that decision and reviews future updates against it. Visual similarity to another shadcn-based interface does not establish equivalent behavior.

## Is shadcn/ui a complete design system?

It can be a foundation for a team's [component library](/glossary/component-libraries.html). A complete [design system](/glossary/design-system.html) also needs product-specific decisions, patterns, content guidance, ownership, and a way to manage changes.

Use the official documentation for installation and the current supported options. Evaluate the components in the actual product context, including any modifications made by people or AI agents.

## Related terms

- [Component Libraries](/glossary/component-libraries.html)
- [AI-ready Design System](/glossary/ai-ready-design-system.html)
- [Headless UI Architecture](/glossary/headless-ui-architecture.html)
- [Model Context Protocol](/glossary/model-context-protocol-mcp.html)

## Sources

- [Introduction, shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs)
- [Registry, shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry)

name: Storybook
definition: Storybook is a frontend tool for developing, documenting, and testing UI components in isolation. A story captures a rendered component in a particular state, such as a form field with a validation error.
contentMarkdown:
# Storybook

Storybook is a frontend tool for developing, documenting, and testing UI components in isolation. A story captures a rendered component in a particular state, such as a form field with a validation error.

## What is a story in Storybook?

A story describes a component example with the inputs and context it needs. Teams can inspect that example without navigating through the entire application.

For a reservation card, useful stories might show a confirmed booking, a canceled booking, a long passenger name, and a missing image. Each example makes a state available for discussion and testing.

Isolation has limits. A card can work in Storybook while its surrounding page has an incorrect reading order or retrieves the wrong reservation. Test complete tasks in the application as well.

## How does Storybook support a design system?

| Use | What the team gets |
|---|---|
| Component development | A place to inspect states and adjust inputs |
| Documentation | Rendered examples with API and usage information |
| Testing | Stories that can support interaction, accessibility, and visual checks |
| Review | A shared view of the implemented component |

The required testing configuration depends on the project. A story's existence does not establish that its interactions or accessibility have been tested.

Storybook can document a [component library](/glossary/component-libraries.html). A [design system](/glossary/design-system.html) also needs shared decisions, usage guidance, ownership, and a way to manage changes.

## What are Storybook MCP and component manifests?

Storybook's AI features let a connected agent access component documentation and work with stories and tests. Its MCP server is one route for that interaction.

A component manifest provides structured information about documented components, including their APIs and examples. A documentation manifest describes documentation content. These are Storybook features, not a universal design system manifest standard.

The AI capabilities are in preview in the documentation checked in November 2026. Component manifests require configuration, and generation differs by framework. Follow the current official guides rather than assuming every existing Storybook exposes this context.

## Example: reviewing an AI-generated field

An agent is asked to add a date field to a booking form. It retrieves the supported component API and examines stories for invalid and unavailable dates. The team reviews the implementation with keyboard input, realistic values, and a failed submission.

The useful outcome is a field that follows the real component contract and works in the task. A convincing preview alone does not establish either result.

## Related terms

- [Design System Documentation](/glossary/design-system-documentation.html)
- [Component Libraries](/glossary/component-libraries.html)
- [Visual Regression Testing](/glossary/visual-regression-testing.html)
- [Model Context Protocol](/glossary/model-context-protocol-mcp.html)

## Sources

- [Why Storybook?, Storybook](https://storybook.js.org/docs/get-started/why-storybook)
- [Using Storybook with AI](https://storybook.js.org/docs/ai)
- [Manifests, Storybook](https://storybook.js.org/docs/ai/manifests)

name: Touch Target Size
definition: Touch target size is the width and height of the area that responds when someone taps or clicks a control. WCAG 2.2 applies its target-size criteria to pointer inputs, including touch and mouse. Measure the interactive area of the control, including any padding that can receive input.
contentMarkdown:
# Touch Target Size

Touch target size is the width and height of the area that responds when someone taps or clicks a control. WCAG 2.2 applies its target-size criteria to pointer inputs, including touch and mouse. Measure the interactive area of the control, including any padding that can receive input.

## What target size does WCAG require?

| WCAG criterion | Minimum target size |
|---|---|
| **2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA** | **24 × 24 CSS pixels**, unless an exception applies. |
| **2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA** | **44 × 44 CSS pixels**, with its own exceptions. |

For the AA spacing exception, place an imaginary circle 24 CSS pixels in diameter at the center of each undersized target’s bounding box. Each circle must avoid overlapping another target or the circle around another undersized target. There are separate exceptions for inline targets, a qualifying equivalent control on the same page, targets sized by the browser without author modification, and essential presentation.

## Example: Edit and delete buttons in a table

A booking table has two 16 × 16 CSS-pixel icon buttons on the same row. Their centers are 20 CSS pixels apart, so their 24-pixel circles overlap. The pair fails the spacing check. Moving their centers to 28 CSS pixels apart clears that overlap for the pair. Check other row actions and nearby targets too.

Another option is to keep each icon at 16 × 16 CSS pixels and add 4 CSS pixels of padding on each side of its button to create a 24 × 24 target. Keep the resulting hit areas separate. In a narrow layout, test the rendered controls with both touch and a mouse so you can tell which action each area triggers.

## Related terms

- [Accessibility and WCAG](/glossary/accessibility-wcag.html)
- [Keyboard Accessibility & Focus Management](/glossary/keyboard-accessibility.html)
- [Zoom, Text Resize & Reflow](/glossary/zoom-text-resize-reflow.html)
- [Design System](/glossary/design-system.html)
- [Web Accessibility Audit](/glossary/web-accessibility-audit.html)

## Sources

name: WCAG Color Contrast
definition: WCAG color contrast measures the difference in relative luminance between two colors. WCAG uses contrast ratios to set minimums for text and for visual information people need to identify interface controls, states, and graphics.
sources: Understanding Use of Color, W3C WAI (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color.html)
contentMarkdown:
# WCAG Color Contrast

WCAG color contrast measures the difference in relative luminance between two colors. WCAG uses contrast ratios to set minimums for text and for visual information people need to identify interface controls, states, and graphics.

## What are the WCAG AA contrast ratios?

| What you are checking | Minimum contrast |
|---|---|
| Standard text and images of text | **4.5:1** against the background under criterion 1.4.3. |
| Large text and images of large text | **3:1** under 1.4.3. Large text is at least 18 pt regular or 14 pt bold, approximately 24 CSS px or 18.7 CSS px, respectively. |
| Visual cues needed to identify a control or state, and parts of graphics needed to understand the content | **3:1** against adjacent colors under criterion 1.4.11, subject to its exceptions. |

Test the rendered foreground against the background it appears on. Placeholder text is subject to the text-contrast requirement. An icon that repeats a visible label may be decorative. For an icon-only button, check the visible icon against its background and give the button an accessible name. Keep a text or shape cue where color alone would convey an error or state.

## Example: Testing a semantic token in two themes

A design system uses `text.secondary` for normal-size text. On a white surface, `#596579` gives a contrast ratio of about **5.90:1**. The same token value on a dark surface, `#171C24`, gives about **2.90:1**, below the 4.5:1 minimum for standard text. Using `#AAB5C5` for `text.secondary` on that dark surface gives about **8.25:1**.

Document which foreground and surface tokens can be paired in each theme. Test those pairs in the components that use them, including relevant states such as errors, selection, and focus. For transparency or gradients, check the actual backgrounds the content can appear against. Use the unrounded ratio for a pass or fail decision.

## Related terms

- [Keyboard Accessibility & Focus Management](/glossary/keyboard-accessibility.html)
- [Design Tokens](/glossary/design-tokens.html)
- [Semantic Tokens](/glossary/semantic-tokens.html)

name: Zoom, Text Resize & Reflow
definition: Page zoom enlarges the rendered page. Text resizing lets people make the text larger. Reflow is how content rearranges to fit the available space so people can read and interact without scrolling in two directions.
contentMarkdown:
# Zoom, Text Resize & Reflow

Page zoom enlarges the rendered page. Text resizing lets people make the text larger. Reflow is how content rearranges to fit the available space so people can read and interact without scrolling in two directions.

## What are the two WCAG checks?

| WCAG criterion | What to verify |
|---|---|
| **1.4.4 Resize Text, Level AA** | Text can be enlarged up to **200%** without loss of content or functionality and without requiring assistive technology. Captions and images of text are exceptions. Browser zoom is one way to provide text resizing. |
| **1.4.10 Reflow, Level AA** | Vertically scrolling content works at a width equivalent to **320 CSS pixels**, without loss of information or functionality or the need to scroll in two directions. For content designed to scroll horizontally, the corresponding height is **256 CSS pixels**. Parts that require a two-dimensional layout for use or meaning are excepted. |

## Example: A booking form with a fare table

At 200% text enlargement, check that field labels and validation errors remain readable and that users can activate the Continue button. At a 320 CSS-pixel width, let the form fields stack and keep the Continue button reachable. If a sticky bar covers errors or makes the remaining viewport too small, let the bar scroll with the form at that layout.

If the fare table needs row and column relationships to make sense, it can scroll within its own region. Keep surrounding content within the page width and let text within individual cells wrap where it can.

## How do you test reflow?

Start with a desktop browser viewport 1,280 CSS pixels wide and zoom to 400% to reach the equivalent of 320 CSS pixels. Check the actual viewport and complete the task, including error recovery. For the separate resize-text check, verify that text can reach twice its original size. If a responsive breakpoint reduces the base font size at higher zoom, compare the resulting visual size with the original.

- [Touch Target Size](/glossary/touch-target-size.html)
